finding_text:
Single Audit Process

Criteria – Under 2 CFR §§200.508 and 200.510, the City is responsible for preparing a complete and accurate Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (SEFA). Under 2 CFR §200.501, a nonfederal entity that expends $1,000,000 or more in federal awards during its fiscal year must obtain a single audit or program-specific audit.

Condition – The City did not maintain a complete listing of federal awards expended during the year ended June 30, 2026. As a result, the initial information provided for the audit did not accurately identify total federal expenditures.

Cause – The City had not established a formal process to identify and track expenditures by federal award throughout the year or to reconcile those expenditures to its accounting records when preparing the SEFA.

Effect – Without a complete and accurate record of federal expenditures, the City may not identify its single audit requirement on a timely basis, and federal programs may be omitted or misstated on the SEFA. No questioned costs were identified as a result of this 
finding.

Recommendation – The City should establish procedures to identify each federal award, record its Assistance Listing number and award information, and track related expenditures throughout the year. At year-end, the City should reconcile those records to its accounting records, prepare the SEFA, and determine whether the single audit threshold has been met before audit planning begins.

Response and Corrective Action Planned – The City will work on a formal process for tracking all federal grants.

Conclusion – Response accepted.

Criteria – Title 2, U.S. Code of Federal Regulations §200.501 states an entity that expends $1,000,000 or more during the non-federal entity’s fiscal year in Federal awards, must have a single audit or program-specific audit conducted for that year in accordance with the provisions in §200.501.

Condition – The City did not provide an accurate listing of federal awards expended even though they were aware of the single audit requirements. 

Cause – The City’s management did not track expenditures of federal awards for the year ended June 30, 2026 to determine what federal audit requirements applied if any. 

Effect – The City’s internal control over compliance with federal audit requirements was inadequate.   

Recommendation – The City should establish a process to track the dollar amount of federal expenditures that were spent during the year to determine if an audit in accordance with uniform guidance is required. This should be done and communicated with the auditors before audit work begins.   

Response and Corrective Action Planned – The City will work on a formal process for tracking all federal grants. 

Conclusion – Response accepted

Finding 2026-001: During the year ended June 30, 2026, the Corporation was delinquent by one monthly mortgage and escrow payment. Additionally, the Corporation incurred late fees as a result of the delinquent mortgage and escrow payment.
Criteria: The Loan Agreement and the Regulatory Agreement with HUD requires the Corporation to make all required monthly mortgage and escrow payments by its due date.
Condition: The Corporation was delinquent one monthly mortgage and escrow payment and additionally, was assessed late fees by the mortgage company due to the delinquency.
Cause: Vacancy and cash flow shortages.
Effect: Noncompliance with HUD regulations and mortgage default.
	Recommendation: We recommend management continue to work to improve occupancy and submit special claim requests to HUD for vacant units to improve cash flow to ensure continued timely payment of the mortgage payments and escrow deposits.
 
Questioned Costs: $1,622

View of Responsible Officials: Management and the board of directors acknowledge the required mortgage payments and escrow deposits were not paid timely in accordance with the Loan Agreement and Regulatory Agreement as required by HUD. Management has been able to fill vacancies and submit special claims to improve cash flow. In July 2025, the Corporation executed a reinstatement agreement with the mortgage lender to make additional monthly mortgage payments of $1,000 through May 2026. The Corporation made an additional principal and interest payment in February 2026 that accelerated the payoff, and the mortgage was brought to current in March 2026. The mortgage lender agreed to waive half of the late fees in April 2026, resulting in a balance due of $1,622 that was paid in May 2026.
